record.body: This tile of the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) seamless products is 1 Arc Second resolution. 3DEP data serve as the elevation layer of The National Map, and provide basic elevation information for Earth science studies and mapping applications in the United States. Scientists and resource managers use 3DEP data for global change research, hydrologic modeling, resource monitoring, mapping and visualization, and many other applications. 3DEP data compose an elevation dataset that consists of seamless layers and a high resolution layer. Each of these layers consists of the best available raster elevation data of the conterminous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, territorial islands, Mexico and Canada. 3DEP data are updated continually as new data become available. Seamless 3DEP data are derived from diverse source data that are processed to a common coordinate system and unit of vertical measure. These data are distributed in geographic coordinates in units of decimal degrees, and in conformance with the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83). All elevation values are in meters and, over the conterminous United States, are referenced to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88). The vertical reference will vary in other areas. Seamless 3DEP data are available nationally (except for Alaska) at resolutions of 1 arc-second (approximately 30 meters) and 1/3 arc-second (approximately 10 meters). In most of Alaska, only lower resolution source data are available. As a result, most seamless 3DEP data for Alaska are at 2 arc-second (approximately 60 meters) grid spacing. Part of Alaska is available at the 1 and 1/3 arc-second resolutions from interferometric synthetic aperture radar (ifsar) collections starting in 2010. Plans are in place for collection of statewide ifsar in Alaska. All 3DEP products are public domain.

record.body: This tile of the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) seamless products is 1 Arc Second resolution. 3DEP data serve as the elevation layer of The National Map, and provide basic elevation information for Earth science studies and mapping applications in the United States. Scientists and resource managers use 3DEP data for global change research, hydrologic modeling, resource monitoring, mapping and visualization, and many other applications. 3DEP data compose an elevation dataset that consists of seamless layers and a high resolution layer. Each of these layers consists of the best available raster elevation data of the conterminous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, territorial islands, Mexico and Canada. 3DEP data are updated continually as new data become available. Seamless 3DEP data are derived from diverse source data that are processed to a common coordinate system and unit of vertical measure. These data are distributed in geographic coordinates in units of decimal degrees, and in conformance with the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83). All elevation values are in meters and, over the conterminous United States, are referenced to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88). The vertical reference will vary in other areas. Seamless 3DEP data are available nationally (except for Alaska) at resolutions of 1 arc-second (approximately 30 meters) and 1/3 arc-second (approximately 10 meters). In most of Alaska, only lower resolution source data are available. As a result, most seamless 3DEP data for Alaska are at 2 arc-second (approximately 60 meters) grid spacing. Part of Alaska is available at the 1 and 1/3 arc-second resolutions from interferometric synthetic aperture radar (ifsar) collections starting in 2010. Plans are in place for collection of statewide ifsar in Alaska. All 3DEP products are public domain.

dataset.title: CHELSA climate moisture index · 1981–2010 normal
dataset.description: One fixed CHELSA V2.1 climate-moisture-index (CMI) mean original for the 1981–2010 climate normal, published by WSL on SWITCH public object storage. According to the authors' dataset paper, CMI is precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration. This historical modeled surface is not current weather, measured soil moisture, annual rainfall, a forecast or air temperature.
dataset.version: CHELSA BIOCLIM+ cmi_mean V2.1 · fixed 1981–2010 climate normal · reviewed 2026-10-12
dataset.attribution: CHELSA / Swiss Federal Research Institute WSL; Brun, P., Zimmermann, N. E., Hari, C., Pellissier, L., and Karger, D. N. (2022), CHELSA-BIOCLIM+, doi:10.16904/envidat.332; dataset-description paper doi:10.5194/essd-14-5573-2022. Distribution: SWITCH public object storage. Preserve cmi_mean, V2.1, the actual 1981–2010 climate normal, source URL and access date.
dataset.nominalResolution: 30 arc-seconds (0.0083333333 degree), approximately 1 km at the equator; ground cell distance varies with latitude
dataset.unit: original Int16 CMI encoding; kg m^-2 month^-1 after embedded scale
dataset.valueInterpretation: Preserve original signed Int16 raw samples, embedded scale 0.1, offset 0 and representable NoData 32767. In the authors' paper, CMI = precipitation - potential evapotranspiration, in kg m^-2 month^-1; physical values require raw × 0.1, separately from raw inspection. Negative values represent a modeled climatic water deficit and positive values a surplus, not observed soil-water content or current drought severity. No automatic conversion, clipping, calibration or resampling is applied.

layers.title: Mean climate moisture index · 1981–2010 normal
layers.unit: raw Int16; kg m^-2 month^-1 after declared scale
layers.valueInterpretation: Original signed CMI mean encoding. Embedded scale 0.1, offset 0, NoData 32767; keep negative samples and the original mask. The authors' paper defines CMI as precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration. It is a 30-year normal, not current soil moisture, rainfall alone, temperature or a single-year observation.

warnings: Only the fixed cmi_mean V2.1 / 1981–2010 original is reviewed. No year or month selection exists. Other climate variables, BIO1 temperature, periods, future scenarios or versions are not substituted; malformed UInt16 files with negative NoData declarations remain unsupported.

The entire published quasi-global original is downloaded without clipping to the requested AOI. A legal WGS84 AOI must intersect the actual distribution. This is a historical downscaled climate normal; it does not establish current conditions, station-level measurement accuracy or exact valid-pixel coverage of the map area.

The original is PixelIsArea, EPSG:4326, 43,200 × 20,880 signed Int16 strip samples with its actual ModelPixelScale/ModelTiepoint. Its outer west/south edges are -180.00013888885002/-90.00013888884999 (a small fraction of a cell beyond the physical world), while all cell centres lie inside. The client query footprint is the intersection with legal physical longitude/latitude; original TIFF bytes, outer extent, transform, grid and click-to-pixel mapping are not rewritten.

Embedded scale is 0.1 and offset is 0. Raw pixel reads remain signed integers: the independently checked Beijing value -323 corresponds to -32.3 kg m^-2 month^-1 only after the documented scale. NoData 32767 is excluded through the original typed declaration, not converted into a physical moisture value. A grayscale thumbnail is not a calibrated climate visualization or a scientific validation.

The author's current climatologies summary describes CMI as a ratio, but its unit is kg m^-2 month^-1 and the original authors' dataset paper explicitly defines precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration. This inconsistency is disclosed. Preserve raw data and consult the authoritative paper (doi:10.5194/essd-14-5573-2022, section 2.2.4) rather than interpreting these samples as a dimensionless ratio.

The independently decoded original includes both valid signed samples and 32767 NoData, including the checked 0-degree ocean position. A numerical value or lack of NoData at a point does not establish scientifically useful land/sea coverage. The original native mask is retained without inventing an ocean mask or a different product's sentinel.
